Microcirculation

Near-infrared exposure increased measured microcirculatory flow in some controlled human studies, including a chronic-wound trial. In a direct comparison, 830-nm near-infrared light increased median flow while 633-nm red light did not. Responses varied, and lasting clinical benefit has not been established.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Controlled human studies report short-term microcirculatory responses under selected protocols, but findings vary by wavelength, population, and endpoint. Near-infrared exposure increased measured flow in several settings, while some red-light or normal-tissue measurements were null.

Summary of the Evidence

Short-term measured flow increased in several controlled studies, including a direct wavelength comparison and a chronic-wound trial. Other studies found no meaningful change in normal-skin oxygenation, and ulcer responses differed by type. The available evidence does not establish a durable clinical benefit.

Human and clinical evidence

In a randomized study of 20 adults, five minutes of 830-nm near-infrared exposure increased median microcirculatory flow by 27%, rising to 54% during the 20-minute follow-up. The 633-nm red-light arm did not increase median flow. Ten participants met the temperature-based response definition. A later waveform analysis reused this cohort rather than testing a new group (Gavish et al. 2020; Ovadia-Blechman et al. 2023).

A randomized double-blind study of 79 people with chronic wounds reported increased blood flow in the active LED groups during eight weeks of treatment. Its comparator received lower-fluence broadband light rather than a passive sham, which limits attribution to PBM alone (Frangez et al. 2017). A sham-controlled study in 30 healthy volunteers found an immediate rise in foot capillary velocity and flux, while an 11-person normal-skin study found no significant oxygenation change after 635-nm red light.

A prospective study assessed 33 wounds in 20 people. Wound-bed temperature rose after PBM in diabetic foot ulcers but not significantly in venous ulcers. Temperature was used as an indirect marker associated with microvascular response, not as a direct flow or wound-healing estimate (Gavish et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

A rabbit experiment reported larger collateral vessels and increased microcirculatory measures after light exposure, whereas a rat wound-healing experiment did not find a significant sustained microcirculatory effect. These models do not establish a response in people with vascular disease.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One human microcirculation publication also included an in-vitro component. The direct evidence is otherwise primarily physiological measurement in people or animals rather than isolated-cell work.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols ranged from a single five-minute exposure to repeated wound treatment. Tested wavelengths included 633–660 nm visible red light and 780–890 nm near-infrared light. Exposure site, baseline temperature, device, and endpoint varied, and no dose or schedule is validated across settings.

Interpretation

Selected studies support acute, protocol-specific changes in measured microcirculation, particularly with near-infrared light. Null findings, responder variation, and indirect endpoints limit generalization. Measured flow or temperature changes do not establish lasting clinical benefit.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

In 20 adults, 830-nm near-infrared exposure increased median microcirculatory flow by 27% during treatment and by 54% during 20-minute follow-up (p=0.049 and p=0.004). The 633-nm red-light arm did not increase median flow; 10 of 20 participants met the temperature-response definition (Gavish et al. 2020).

In 79 people with chronic wounds, microcirculation increased within the treated diabetic and non-diabetic groups (p=0.040 and p=0.033), while no significant change was reported in the broadband-light reference groups. The accessible summary does not provide a between-group effect magnitude (Frangez et al. 2017).

In 20 people with 33 ulcers, wound-bed temperature changed by +2.10 ± 2.25 °C in diabetic foot ulcers (p<0.001) and +0.68 ± 2.49 °C in venous ulcers (p=0.385). This was an indirect thermal measure, not a direct flow estimate (Gavish et al. 2026).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for acute measured flow changes in selected human settings.

Low for consistent responses across settings or lasting clinical benefit.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Several controlled human experiments found acute flow increases after near-infrared exposure, but results varied by wavelength, person, site, and endpoint. Red-light and normal-tissue studies included null findings, and a thermal response is not the same as a clinical outcome. Repeated trials linking flow changes to healing or symptoms would be needed for stronger certainty.
